title: Washing crochet garments: using care labels
subtitle: How to read yarn care symbols and apply them to finished crochet garments
excerpt: Yarn care symbols appear on yarn labels and indicate the safe washing, drying, and ironing methods for that fibre. Reading the symbols on the yarn used in a finished garment tells you exactly how to wash it without damage. Washing a wool garment in a hot machine wash or tumble-drying an acrylic garment on high heat causes irreversible damage. A minute reading the care label prevents it.
sourceNotes: Pauline Turner, How to Crochet (HarperCollins). Edie Eckman, The Crochet Answer Book (Storey Publishing).

glossaryTerms.definition: An internationally standardised icon on a yarn label (or garment care label) indicating the safe maximum washing temperature, whether tumble drying is permitted, whether ironing is safe, and whether dry cleaning is permitted. Based on the ISO 3758 standard.

Wool treated to remove or coat the scales on each fibre that cause felting. Superwash-treated wool can usually be machine-washed at a low temperature, unlike untreated wool which felts irreversibly in the machine.

content.text: Care symbols

on yarn labels are internationally standardised: a washing tub icon for wash temperature, a square with a circle for tumble drying, an iron for ironing temperature, and a circle for dry cleaning. Every yarn label carries these symbols. Before washing a finished garment, find the labels from the yarn used and follow the care symbols on them.
Common care symbols and what they mean
Washing tub with 30: machine wash at a maximum of 30°C.
Washing tub with a hand inside: hand wash only.
Washing tub with an X through it: do not wash in water. Dry clean only.
Square with a circle and an X: do not tumble dry.
Iron with one dot: cool iron, 110°C maximum. Suitable for synthetic fibres.
Iron with two dots: warm iron, 150°C maximum. Suitable for wool and silk.
Iron with an X: do not iron.
Common fibre types and typical care
Untreated wool: hand wash at 30°C maximum. Do not tumble dry. Lay flat to dry.
Superwash wool
can be machine-washed on a wool or delicate cycle at 30°C.
Acrylic: most acrylics are machine-washable at 30 to 40°C. Do not steam block. Low tumble dry (if label permits).
Cotton: machine-washable at 40 to 60°C. Shrinks at high temperatures. Can be tumble-dried on low.
Silk and mohair: hand wash at 30°C. Never tumble dry. Lay flat to dry.
Wool-acrylic blends: follow the more delicate fibre's rules. If the blend is 70% acrylic and 30% wool, treat it as wool and hand wash.
Common problems

items.symptom: A wool garment has felted and shrunk irreversibly in the machine
items.cause: Untreated wool was washed in a hot machine with agitation. Heat and movement cause the fibre scales to lock together.
items.fix: There is no way to undo felting. The felted fabric can be repurposed: cut it into flat pieces (it will not fray) for patchwork or embroidery. Future pieces: check the label for superwash treatment.

items.symptom: An acrylic garment has distorted and become permanently stretched after tumble drying
items.cause: Acrylic fibres soften under heat and can stretch or distort if tumbled at a high temperature.
items.fix: Lay the garment flat while damp and reshape to the correct dimensions. Pin if necessary. Let it dry flat. Do not apply heat to acrylic to restore shape.

content.text: What to try next

Keep the ball band from the yarn used in each finished garment in a small envelope stapled to the pattern or project notes. Years after making the garment, the care instructions will still be readable. Writing the care instructions on the project notes page directly is also good practice: ball bands detach and get lost, but project notes are usually kept alongside the garment itself.
